title: Palmer Penguins: An R Analysis
text: This post examines how body mass and bill length vary across the three species in the Palmer Penguins dataset. The data come from the Palmer Penguins project and were collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station, Antarctica LTER. The dataset is released under the CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication. It is included in the palmerpenguins R package, so rendering this post does not download a separate data file.

title: Palmer Penguins: An R Analysis
text:
Prepare the data

library(palmerpenguins)
library(tidyverse)

Removing rows with missing values

analysis_penguins <- penguins |>
  drop_na(species, bill_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex)

tibble(
  original_rows = nrow(penguins),
  complete_rows = nrow(analysis_penguins)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  original_rows complete_rows
          <int>         <int>
1           344           333

title: Palmer Penguins: An R Analysis
text:
Compare the species
Then we calculate the sample size and mean body measurements for each species.



Table 1: Sample size and mean body measurements by penguin species.


species_summary <- analysis_penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    mean_bill_length_mm = mean(bill_length_mm),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("mean_"), ~ round(.x, 1)))

species_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species       n mean_body_mass_g mean_bill_length_mm
  <fct>     <int>            <dbl>               <dbl>
1 Adelie      146            3706.                38.8
2 Chinstrap    68            3733.                48.8
3 Gentoo      119            5092.                47.6




Gentoo penguins are substantially heavier on average: approximately 5,092 g, compared with 3,706 g for Adelie and 3,733 g for Chinstrap penguins. Chinstrap penguins have the longest mean bill at approximately 48.8 mm.
The figure compares bill length with body mass. Colour separates the species, making both the between-species differences and the within-species trends visible.

ggplot(
  analysis_penguins,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







Figure 1: Bill length and body mass for Palmer Penguins, coloured by species.





To quantify those within-species trends, I calculate the correlation between bill length and body mass separately for each species.



Table 2: Correlation between bill length and body mass within each species.


species_correlations <- analysis_penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(correlation = round(correlation, 3))

species_correlations

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   correlation
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Adelie          0.544
2 Chinstrap       0.514
3 Gentoo          0.667




Bill length and body mass are positively corelated within all three species. The relationship is strongest for Gentoo penguins (correlation 0.667), followed by Adelie (0.544) and Chinstrap penguins (0.514). Overall, species explains a difference in typical body mass, while bill length still provides useful information about how it is corealted with body mass within each species.

title: Palmer Penguins: A Python Analysis
text:
Compare the species
Then we calculate the sample size and mean body measurements for each species.

species_summary = (
    analysis_penguins.groupby("species", observed=True)
    .agg(
        n=("species", "size"),
        mean_body_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"),
        mean_bill_length_mm=("bill_length_mm", "mean"),
    )
    .round(1)
)

Gentoo penguins are much heavier on average: about 5,092 g compared with about 3,706 g for Adelie and 3,733 g for Chinstrap penguins. Chinstrap penguins have the longest mean bill at approximately 48.8 mm.
The following figure is generated directly from the summary table. It uses an inline SVG so that the analysis does not require an additional plotting package.

plot_data = species_summary.reset_index()
width, height = 700, 420
left, top, plot_height = 90, 35, 300
bar_width = 120
gap = 80
maximum = plot_data["mean_body_mass_g"].max()
colours = ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73"]

elements = [
    f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{width}" height="{height}" '
    f'viewBox="0 0 {width} {height}">',
    '<style>text { font-family: sans-serif; fill: #222; }</style>',
    f'<line x1="{left}" y1="{top}" x2="{left}" y2="{top + plot_height}" '
    'stroke="#333"/>',
    f'<line x1="{left}" y1="{top + plot_height}" x2="{width - 35}" '
    f'y2="{top + plot_height}" stroke="#333"/>',
]

for index, row in plot_data.iterrows():
    x = left + 60 + index * (bar_width + gap)
    bar_height = row["mean_body_mass_g"] / maximum * plot_height
    y = top + plot_height - bar_height
    elements.extend(
        [
            f'<rect x="{x}" y="{y:.1f}" width="{bar_width}" '
            f'height="{bar_height:.1f}" fill="{colours[index]}"/>',
            f'<text x="{x + bar_width / 2}" y="{y - 8:.1f}" '
            f'text-anchor="middle">{row["mean_body_mass_g"]:.0f} g</text>',
            f'<text x="{x + bar_width / 2}" y="{top + plot_height + 25}" '
            f'text-anchor="middle">{row["species"]}</text>',
        ]
    )

elements.extend(
    [
        f'<text x="20" y="{top + plot_height / 2}" '
        'transform="rotate(-90 20 185)" text-anchor="middle">'
        'Mean body mass (g)</text>',
        '</svg>',
    ]
)

display(SVG(data="".join(elements)))







Figure 1: Mean body mass of Palmer Penguins by species.





To quantify those within-species trends, I calculate the correlation between bill length and body mass separately for each species.

species_correlations = (
    analysis_penguins.groupby("species", observed=True)
    .apply(
        lambda group: group["bill_length_mm"].corr(group["body_mass_g"]),
        include_groups=False,
    )
    .rename("correlation")
    .round(3)
    .to_frame()
)

title: About
text:
I’m a software engineer and data science graduate student with a background spanning embedded systems, machine learning, and AI systems.
Before starting my Master of Data Science at the University of British Columbia, I worked at Qualcomm on system-level software for complex SoC platforms, where I dealt with low-level integration, boot flows, debugging, and reliability. Alongside this, I built automation and internal developer tools—including AI-assisted workflows—to make large-scale debugging and analysis faster and more efficient.


My interests increasingly sit at the intersection of software systems and artificial intelligence: building AI agents with memory, graph-based retrieval systems, intelligent developer tools, and systems that can reason over complex information rather than simply generate text.
I enjoy understanding how things work from the lowest levels of hardware and operating systems all the way up to modern AI applications. Most of my projects reflect that curiosity—combining engineering, experimentation, and practical problem solving to build systems that are actually useful.
I’m currently exploring data science, AI systems, and intelligent software while continuing to build projects around agents, retrieval, memory, and scalable automation.
